packets.key_finding: A field-experiment nudge that discourages minimum-only credit-card payments cut minimum-only paying by 23% at six months but did not significantly reduce debt, because nudged cardholders mostly chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum and liquidity-constrained cardholders were disproportionately affected.
packets.methodology: Field experiment with credit card issuer, six-month follow-up on payment and debt outcomes; abstract gives effect sizes.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's objection in a real consumer financial product: a nudge changed a nominal enrollment-like metric while leaving the real outcome (debt/savings) unmoved, and hurt liquidity-constrained users most \u2014 exactly the enrollment-vs-amount and distributional questions the brief asks about.
limitations: credit card debt paydown, not a savings product
six-month horizon only
US regulatory context, not EU
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer financial product field RCT showing enrollment-metric change without real behavioral change, with a liquidity-driven distributional finding.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges on risk-taking have medium-to-large effects, but implementing a default nudge \u2014 and especially having individuals refuse it \u2014 lowers users' rating of the advice/advisor, and framing of the default presentation shifts chosen allocations.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country EU sample, manipulating default presence and framing of a financial-allocation decision.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives EU-context evidence that a financial default can be perceived as manipulative and damage trust when refused, directly bearing on the dark-pattern/reputational risk question, and shows framing of the default choice anchors the amount chosen \u2014 relevant to how to phrase the multiplier default.
limitations: risk-allocation/investment decision rather than round-up savings specifically
wealth-manager advice framing, not a self-serve app flow
effect on trust measured via ratings, not actual complaints or churn
packets.relevance_reason: Recent EU-sample experimental evidence directly on when a financial default reads as manipulative versus helpful, and on framing-driven anchoring \u2014 exactly the manipulation-risk and anchoring questions in the brief.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage rose 113% on iOS and 12% on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with the effect persisting at least 15 months post-rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design around the staggered EU DMA choice-screen mandate on iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: The most directly comparable EU evidence on whether an active-choice screen can substantially shift behaviour away from an incumbent default, with the effect measured well past initial rollout — central to the active-choice-vs-default decision.
limitations: studies browser choice, not financial contribution decisions
cross-platform differences (iOS vs Android rollout) complicate a single effect-size estimate
packets.relevance_reason: Best available recent EU evidence quantifying an active-choice mandate's effect on real behaviour, with persistence beyond a year.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default savings-rate auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of those defaulted into escalation actually escalate on the first date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, vesting, withdrawal-on-separation, and opt-out from auto-escalation.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest statement of our support team's objection: the enrollment lift is real at signup and much smaller once job turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for, meaning enrollment numbers can be a vanity metric relative to actual amounts saved.
limitations: retirement plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting
US 401(k) institutional specifics may not map onto app defaults
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving once medium/long-run attrition is accounted for, which the brief explicitly asked us to look for.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign sites raised donations by over $43 million but also increased refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on small, first-time donors who likely did not intend the recurring commitment.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across multiple 2020 U.S. campaign websites exploiting different rollout timing of pre-checked recurring-donation boxes.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a real quantified case of a recurring-contribution default producing unintended enrolment and elevated 'refunds' (a direct analogue to complaints/withdrawals) concentrated among naive users — precisely the support team's worry, with dollar figures attached.
limitations: political donations, not a banking savings product
no 6–12 month persistence tracking beyond refund requests
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative case of a recurring-contribution default causing disproportionate harm to inexperienced, small-scale users.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when and how default choice architecture produces downstream (persistent) effects on consumer behavior, identifying time course, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
packets.methodology: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis of the consumer-defaults literature building a research agenda; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the project a framework for exactly the question it needs answered \u2014 whether the round-up default will persist or fade \u2014 by naming the conditions (salience, antecedent preference strength) under which defaults do or don't stick, which should shape what to measure post-launch.
limitations: conceptual/theoretical, not a new empirical estimate
no specific effect sizes
not focused on financial products specifically
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest general-consumer (non-employer) synthesis of when default effects persist versus decay, directly informing the persistence question.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrolment into just-in-time overdraft alerts cuts unarranged overdraft charges 17–19% and arranged charges 4–8%, worth £170–240 million market-wide, though users still capture less than half of available savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale field experiments at major UK banks testing automatic enrolment into SMS alerts.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world analogue to our feature: a consumer bank testing automatic enrolment into a low-friction financial nudge at scale, with real behavioural and monetary effect sizes — sets the benchmark our own default-effect measurement should be compared against.
limitations: studies alerts, not a savings/contribution feature per se
no explicit 6–12 month persistence analysis reported
packets.relevance_reason: Directly relevant, same-sector (UK banking), automatic-enrolment field evidence with quantified financial outcomes.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, all tested nudges — including default options — significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, with the largest backfire from positive-narrative and default-option nudges, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, default-option, and narrative nudges on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise the brief asks us to test, with an RCT rather than an anecdote, and shows the effect can reverse depending on cultural/institutional trust — exactly the kind of evidence needed before defaulting everyone in.
limitations: hypothetical/survey-based willingness rather than real enrolment behaviour
Chinese voluntary-pension context, not an EU consumer savings app
small sample (n=220)
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest counter-evidence in this batch that a default can reduce rather than raise savings intentions, fulfilling the brief's explicit call for a contradicting study.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: This NBER review synthesizes household-finance behavior and the choice-architecture interventions (defaults, product design, disclosure) that firms and governments use to shape financial outcomes, drawing on the behavioral economics literature on consumption and saving.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and intervention evidence in household finance.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the synthesis-level view the brief asks for (a review giving effect-size context) across consumer financial behavior broadly, useful for calibrating how much weight to put on any single default study and where our round-up decision sits in the wider choice-architecture toolkit.
limitations: broad narrative review, not systematic protocol
not specific to fintech round-up products
authored by the same team behind the classic 401(k) default studies, so may overweight retirement-plan evidence
packets.relevance_reason: Serves as the review/meta-level synthesis the brief explicitly wants alongside single-study estimates.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: In a randomized experiment on salary-linked savings accounts in Afghanistan, default enrollment increased participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven mainly by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it also shifted attitudes toward saving.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment assigning employees to different default/enrollment varieties of a salary-linked savings account, with follow-up interventions isolating mechanisms.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, causally identified effect size for the default effect on enrollment and, crucially, explains the mechanism (present bias, cognitive cost) — informing whether the lift from an opt-out design in our app is likely to be real behavior change or mere inertia, and whether it persists in attitudes afterward.
limitations: salary-linked account for employees, not a self-directed mobile banking app
developing-country context, different regulatory and liquidity environment
no long-run (6-12 month) withdrawal or amount-saved data reported
packets.relevance_reason: Rare experimental evidence quantifying the default effect size and its causal mechanism, directly bearing on whether enrollment gains are genuine engagement or inertia.
packets.title: Why Do Defaults Affect Behavior? Experimental Evidence from Afghanistan
packets.abstract: We report on an experiment examining why default options impact behavior. By randomly assigning employees to different varieties of a salary-linked savings account, we find that default enrollment increases participation by 40 percentage points—an effect equivalent to providing a 50 percent matching incentive. We then use a series of experimental interventions to differentiate between explanations for the default effect, which we conclude is driven largely by present-biased preferences and the cognitive cost of thinking through different savings scenarios. Default assignment also changes employees’ attitudes toward saving, and makes them more likely to actively decide to save after the study concludes. (JEL C93, D14, D91, O12)

alternates.key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, people generally approve of financial 'nudges,' with strong preferences for System 2 (deliberative) interventions and savings-framed interventions, and approval did not depend on transparency or on whether a bank was the messenger.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered vignette survey with 36 hypothetical financial-intervention scenarios, varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting; representative Australian sample, six dependent variables including manipulation and likelihood of bank-proposed use.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests the reputational risk the brief flags: whether an opt-out/default design in a bank app reads as helpful or manipulative, and shows savings-framed, transparent, deliberative defaults are best received — evidence for how to frame the entry decision, not just whether to default.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not real enrollment behavior
no measure of persistence or actual amounts saved
Australian sample, not EU
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly addresses consumer perception of financial defaults as manipulative vs. helpful, the EU dark-pattern reputational concern named in the brief.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: An opt-in short-term, withdraw-anytime savings account offered via payroll deduction at five UK firms saw only 0.7% of eligible employees ever activate an account, but among those who did, 96% still had a positive balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at month 12.
alternates.methodology: Field study of a choice-architecture intervention at five UK firms tracking account activation and 12-month usage among an opt-in short-term savings product.
alternates.why_it_matters: The closest existing empirical analog to the round-up pot itself \u2014 a liquid, withdraw-anytime savings product under opt-in \u2014 giving real numbers on the opt-in take-up/engagement trade-off: very low uptake but strong persistence and continued contribution among those who join, directly informing what to expect from an opt-in design.
limitations: enrollment channel is payroll deduction at an employer, not a standalone app
UK firms only, five-firm sample
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice arms in this specific study
alternates.relevance_reason: Same liquid short-term savings product structure as the round-up feature, giving direct opt-in take-up and 12-month persistence numbers rather than a retirement-plan analogy.
alternates.title: Employer-Based Short-Term Savings Accounts
alternates.abstract: We study the introduction of a choice architecture design intended to increase short-term savings among employees at five U.K. firms. Employees were offered the opportunity to opt into a payroll deduction program that auto-deposits funds from each paycheck into a short-term savings account from which withdrawals are possible at any time. We find that employees who opted into the program kept using it. Among employees whose accounts were created early enough to be observed over the first 12 months after their account activation and who did not separate from employment during this period, 96% still had a balance greater than 1 and 87% received an automatic payroll contribution in month 12. However, product take-up was very low: no more than 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account. Opt-in access to short-term savings programs does not elicit widespread participation.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (forcing a yes/no decision, no default) and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option are effective alternatives to automatic enrollment for motivating behavior change.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against opt-out/no-default conditions, reviewing prior automatic-enrollment savings applications.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly informs the entry-design decision by testing the exact 'active choice' alternative the brief is weighing against opt-in/opt-out, including a specific enhanced variant that could recover most of the enrollment benefit of a default without full passive enrollment.
limitations: primary field tests are in medication adherence, not financial products
does not report persistence at 6-12 months for savings behavior specifically
no amount-saved outcome
alternates.relevance_reason: The originating study and only source directly comparing active choice/enhanced active choice against defaults, the mechanism the brief names as decision 1's third option.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million tipping decisions shows default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (84% of adherence needs both), and adding a lower preset option (15%) below an existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at low revenue cost.
alternates.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey; counterfactual menu-design simulation.
alternates.why_it_matters: The specific technique here \u2014 decomposing why a preset menu of options anchors choices, and simulating how adding/removing a preset level changes both the chosen level and welfare \u2014 is exactly the analysis needed to decide whether to ship a 1x/2x/5x multiplier menu and which value to pre-select.
limitations: setting is tip percentages on taxi rides, not savings contributions
no persistence/withdrawal outcomes measured
welfare framework is revenue-focused, not consumer-protection focused
alternates.relevance_reason: Method directly transferable to the multiplier-menu design decision: structural decomposition of why a preset level anchors choice and how changing the menu shifts outcomes.
alternates.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
alternates.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

alternates.key_finding: Maps EU law on dark patterns to a taxonomy of six autonomy-violation categories, framing regulation as protection of consumer autonomy rather than a blanket ban on defaults.
alternates.methodology: Legal doctrinal analysis and taxonomy-building across EU consumer-protection law; abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the actual EU legal test for when a default or pre-selection crosses from helpful into a sanctionable dark pattern, which is exactly the reputational-risk question the opt-out design raises.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or amounts
no direct evidence on savings-app behaviour
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides the EU regulatory framework for judging whether an opt-out round-up default would read as manipulative, directly bearing on the entry-design decision.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.
